title: The Max Headroom Incident
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the Max Headroom character, from the 1985 movie and the 1987 TV series about a future where TV networks rule and "blip vert" ads cause viewers to explode, to the November 1987 Chicago broadcast signal intrusions in which a man in a Max Headroom mask hijacked WGN and PBS station WTTW's signals during a Bears sportscast and a Doctor Who episode. They cover the bizarre content of the intrusion, the FCC and FBI investigation, the technical theory of how it was done with microwave transmission, the suspects (Eric Fournier and Bowie Pogue) and why the case remains unsolved. The episode closes with a listener mail about the Allman Brothers album Eat a Peach and a sign-off.

segments.title: Live show announcements
segments.summary: Hosts promote upcoming live tour dates in Salt Lake City, Phoenix, Melbourne, Perth and Brisbane, with tickets at sysk live.

segments.title: Introduction and Motherboard source
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode and credit Alex Pasternak's Motherboard article on the Max Headroom incident as the main source.

segments.title: What Max Headroom was
segments.summary: Max Headroom was a computer-generated style talk show host played by Matt Frewer in makeup, starting with the 1985 movie and a TV series. He appeared in a New Coke ad with Run DMC and was a cult figure among cyberpunks and geeks.

segments.title: Max Headroom TV series plot
segments.summary: In the series' future, TV networks rule the world and use blip verts, short fast ads, which cause viewers to explode. Reporter Edison Carter is left in a coma after seeing a sign reading Max Headroom 2.3 meters, and his brain is uploaded to create an AI, which pirate broadcasters later use as Max Headroom.

segments.title: Special effects and makeup
segments.summary: Because computer graphics were not available, the Max Headroom effect used prosthetic makeup, with a four-hour process applied to Matt Frewer; Letterman interview segments were staged with Frewer in another studio.

segments.title: Chicago broadcast intrusion, November 1987
segments.summary: During a WGN sportscast on the evening after the Bears beat the Lions, Dan Roan's broadcast was interrupted by a man in a Max Headroom mask with no audio for about eleven seconds. Engineers switched to a backup transmitter. About two hours later, WTTW's Doctor Who broadcast was interrupted for about a minute and twenty-two seconds.

segments.title: Content of the second intrusion
segments.summary: The masked man, on a warped, rocking corrugated metal background, garbled his speech, mocked WGN and sportscaster Chuck Swirsky, referenced a 'marital aid', drank New Coke, hummed the Clutch Cargo theme, and was spanked with a fly swatter by a person in a bonnet. Reactions from Chicago residents were aired on WGN.

segments.title: FCC and FBI investigation
segments.summary: The FCC got involved, and the offense was a felony with fines and jail time possible. Early investigators assumed it required expensive equipment and high electricity, but Dr. Michael Marcus said a cheap setup on a nearby rooftop could have overpowered the microwave link. The FBI enhanced video frames, but the investigation went cold and no one was charged; the statute of limitations expired.

segments.title: Suspects and the unsolved mystery
segments.summary: Early online bulletin board posts described the method two days after the event. Two suspects are discussed: Eric Fournier, whose friends denied involvement, and Bowie Pogue, who recalled older Chicago geeks, possibly including a man and his brother, hinting at a big event on the day. Nobody has been confirmed responsible.

segments.title: Listener mail: Eat a Peach
segments.summary: A listener notes that Dwayne Allman's 'eat a peach for peace' remark may be the origin of the Allman Brothers album title Eat a Peach.
